I have often told my students:

> **Writing is like paving a highway from your brain to the reader.**

You know your research intimately.

You remember why the problem interested you, which approaches failed, why you changed the experiment, what surprised you in the results, and how you eventually reached your conclusion.

The reader knows none of this.

Scientific writing therefore has a very practical purpose:

> **Build a sufficiently clear road so that another researcher can travel from your question to your conclusion.**

For many years, I have summarized what I expect from a research paper using three words:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Creativity}
\quad+\quad
\text{Consistency}
\quad+\quad
\text{Completeness}
}
$$

I call this the **CCC rule**.

These three requirements apply not only to individual sentences. They apply to the entire research paper.

---

## The CCC rule

### Creativity

A paper must contain something worth communicating.

That usually means something **new**:

- a new theory,
- a new method,
- new experimental evidence,
- a new application,
- a new interpretation,
- an unexpected mechanism,
- or a useful extension of an existing principle.

The key word for publication is therefore

$$
\boxed{\text{NEW}.}
$$

Creativity does not necessarily mean inventing an entirely new field.

A new interpretation of an existing phenomenon may be scientifically important.

A known principle applied successfully to a difficult engineering problem may also be valuable.

But the reader should be able to answer:

> **What do I know after reading this paper that I did not know before?**

---

### Consistency

Every part of the paper must belong to the same research story.

The chain should look like

$$
\boxed{
\text{Title}
\rightarrow
\text{Abstract}
\rightarrow
\text{Question}
\rightarrow
\text{Method}
\rightarrow
\text{Results}
\rightarrow
\text{Discussion}
\rightarrow
\text{Conclusions}.
}
$$

The title should describe the work that is actually presented.

The abstract should summarize the same work.

The results should answer the question posed in the introduction.

The conclusions should be supported by those results.

Figures and tables should contain the same data reported in the text.

Symbols, terminology, units, and definitions should remain consistent throughout the manuscript.

A paper should behave like **one system**, not several sections written independently.

---

### Completeness

Completeness does not mean including everything that happened during the research.

It means including everything the reader needs in order to understand and verify the argument.

Thus,

$$
\boxed{
\text{Completeness}
\neq
\text{maximum amount of information}.
}
$$

Instead,

$$
\boxed{
\text{Completeness}
=
\text{no essential gap between question and conclusion}.
}
$$

A paper may be short and complete.

It may also be long and incomplete.

This distinction is important.

---

## Why publish at all?

Research has limited value to the scientific community until it is communicated.

A published article creates a record of

- what problem was studied,
- what was discovered,
- how the result was obtained,
- and what contribution was made.

Publication also allows other researchers to

- examine the work,
- challenge it,
- reproduce it,
- improve it,
- and build upon it.

A conference paper and a journal article may serve different purposes.

A conference presentation may introduce work in progress or stimulate discussion.

A journal article should normally provide a more complete, durable account of the research.

Publication is therefore not merely an administrative step after doing research.

It is part of the research process itself.

---

## Before writing: is there actually a paper?

Before worrying about English, LaTeX, journal format, or figure placement, I ask several more fundamental questions.

### Is there a creative contribution?

Can I say clearly what is new?

For example:

> We discovered that...

> We developed...

> We demonstrated...

> We found that the conventional assumption fails when...

> We provide a new interpretation of...

If the novelty cannot be stated clearly, the research story may not yet be mature.

### Are the results reproducible?

For experimental work, another researcher should be able to understand the materials, specimens, loading conditions, equipment, measurements, and processing needed to reproduce the essential results.

For theoretical or computational work, the hypotheses, assumptions, governing equations, numerical procedures, boundary conditions, and validation should be clear enough to reproduce the analysis.

### Are the results consistent?

Check whether

- repeated tests agree reasonably,
- numerical trends are physically credible,
- tables and figures agree,
- units are consistent,
- reported values do not change between sections,
- and the explanation is compatible with the evidence.

### Is the logic complete?

Can the reader follow the reasoning without being asked to make an unsupported jump?

These questions already contain the CCC rule.

---

## A research paper is a story

A paper is not simply a container for everything produced during a project.

It is a story with a particular structure:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Question}
\rightarrow
\text{Effort to answer}
\rightarrow
\text{Answer}.
}
$$

For an engineering paper, I would expand this slightly:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Problem}
\rightarrow
\text{Question}
\rightarrow
\text{Method}
\rightarrow
\text{Evidence}
\rightarrow
\text{Interpretation}
\rightarrow
\text{Engineering meaning}.
}
$$

This is more useful than beginning with the conventional headings

```text
Introduction
Methods
Results
Conclusions
